title: Game dev takes time, even with AI! 8+ months into my project
author: Kashmakers
selftext:
I've been a game dev for the past 10 years. I started using AI to code my next game last year. It's been 8 months at this point, I've got no playable demo, barely any screenshots to share, but I've finished *so much* infrastructure underneath it. And honestly, that's just how game dev goes.

It takes time, you know. Oneshotting with AI just means you're getting AI slop. Game dev is about decisions, art direction and design, and the AI is definitely useful, but it doesn't replace your vision.

So don't be discouraged if you see a really awesome gameplay video of someone saying "I vibe coded this in a week" and feel like you're behind somehow. A real playable game still takes a long time to develop.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Nah, for most people in the sub their web of systems and code is likely some nebulous mess they don't even tangentally understand. I can only imagine the tech debt, which makes actually testing for and smashing out bugs incredibly difficult. Either that, or the game itself is very simple. Throwing someone an avatar with 6 basic things it can do is far easier to keep a lid on while broadly vibing everything than, say, deckbuilder combat with 400 different cards that leverage 50 different core mechanics. Likewise a single scene in your game where everything takes place is very different when it comes to managing than a procedurally genned open world.

So some of this comes down to scope. But the simpler a game, the more I'd expect a crazy coat of paint and perfect polish, both of which are AI's weakest fronts, for things like visual/audio stimulation and reward feedback in order to keep somebody's interest.

comments.author: oadephon
comments.body:
Exactly, man. I'm like 5 months deep in consistent work and it's just been endless iterations. You try something, it kind of works, and you tweak it, or you redesign it completely. One system in my game has already gone through like 5 redesigns. One UI screen went through around 10 redesigned before landing on something decent *enough* to play the game without tons of friction, but it **still** has issues. AI speeds up the process of iteration by so much, but making a good game is still such an immense process.

And I like to brainstorm with AI, too. You always come away with 12 ideas to reject and 1 idea that's kind of shaped right but where the details are wrong, and you iterate on it over and over.

There's no shortcut to a good game design. Everything is kind of path-dependent as you chip away at the parts that don't work. It's very satisfying, but it still takes forever.

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
> One system in my game has already gone through like 5 redesigns.

I feel this haha. It's 8+ months for me and I still don't have the inventory UI finished. Mostly because I've redesigned how it should look like several times and have only just settled on a final design. It really do be like that sometimes.

> And I like to brainstorm with AI, too. You always come away with 12 ideas to reject and 1 idea that's kind of shaped right but where the details are wrong, and you iterate on it over and over.

Treating the AI agent as a buddy to brainstorm is one of its best uses. Even just using it as a rubber duck method; I find myself getting a lot more clarity trying to explain a system and what I want to happen, and I start realizing my own edge cases. AI is great for that, and it helps you point out other things you may have forgotten.

Are you blocked by the AI not being productive or by you needing time to flesh out your ideas?

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
Mine is a farming sim. Basically, I have a strict vision and how I want systems to work, so I've been focused on one small thing after another. The farming system itself was the easiest part lol. It's the NPC path finding, schedules, dialogue, animations etc. that took up a huge chunk of my time (AI cannot make my animations). I also create a lot of tools for myself to make my workflow easier.

There's also the part that as I continue to develop, I refactor many older systems since they need new functions. My item database is one such thing; always being reworked to add one more thing, change another, maybe delete a parameter.

This month alone I spent all my time on simply animations for my characters. I draw all the art myself.

When it comes to pure systems alone - just code - AI can whip that up in a minute. But if it needs input from me, especially visual input, it can take much longer.

replies.author: IcyBother8850
replies.body: Thanks for the long response it really puts things into perspective. Honestly the artsy stuff is a huge timesink for me too, just normalizing models in blender takes me ungodly ammount of time...

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
It's the price of gamedev! Some days I do nothing but draw a shirt a hundred times.

It's why progress is slow, even with AI. But to be fair, I wouldn't have been able to get this far without AI. AI allows me to no longer think "I think this would be cool, but I don't know how to make it." and instead, I think "I have a cool idea! Let's use AI to see how we can add it to the game and make it work."

So in essence, you end up adding more complex mechanics to your game that you otherwise wouldn't have done without AI, extending the development time.

replies.author: IcyBother8850
replies.body: I really like that way of using AI too. Its not about using AI to make a simple game fast its about using AI to push to the limit of what is possible for a single dev to achieve in regards of complexity and scope.

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
Exactly! AI allows you to no longer be constricted. AI is great for people who already have a great vision for their game, so they can utilize it and actually start building it.

Only twice have I encountered legitimate setbacks for a mechanic I wanted in the game, and it's not the AI's fault - it's engine restricted. But so far, everything I've thrown at it, it was able to create and it works.

To me, the fun parts are creating tools for myself so I can develop the game using my own interface and language. Like creating your own item database. But that's just me lol.

comments.author: KoodiRonsu
comments.body: Any kind of design takes about the same amount of time as it would without AI. So that part of development won't benefit from the AI. The coding part of development usually becomes much larger than it would without AI, because AI can quickly pump out fairly usable quality code if you have the technical knowledge and experience to look after what its doing and to make important decisions for it. Then you can create much more complete/larger systems than  you would have tried to do without AI. So that in itself slows down the project back to about the same speed as if you weren't using AI at all.

replies.author: Kashmakers

It's pretty close though after 8 months! But there's no 'rule' to follow here; pushing for a demo is good, but what you really want is player feedback. And you can get player feedback without relying on a demo (players tend to view demos negatively if they are not 100% polished and don't reflect the actual game).

replies.author: thefox828
replies.body:
Well usually you start an AI session with planning mode, sketch out all the details and then let the AI write a design document in markdown. Then you should go through it line by line and really think if it is what you want, if there is something not written or missing or if there is something which is overhead or too much.  
There are also skills out there for spec driven development or obra/superpowers on github which change the way the AI interacts with you, like really starts asking you a lot more details.  
Finally the planning phase, even if it consumes more time in the first place, pays off by saving you iterations down the road.

replies.author: Kashmakers

> Meanwhile I'm a month into my project and it's maybe %5 done.

Lol, you sure about that? I'm 8 months into mine, and I don't think I can pinpoint how much is 'completed' yet. I'd sort it into two sections; core systems, and content. Content is what players will play; the story, the characters, the progress. Core systems is your gameplay (to be fair, it's possible you don't have story content and you legit have a racing game or something), such as fighting, wall jumping, smashing crates etc. For me, I'd say my core systems are at 60%, and my content is at 0%.

Game dev takes longer than it looks like.

comments.author: Big_Froyo5581
comments.body:
I'm glad this was posted... I've also spent 8+ months (with AI) building modulatarity via boring but powerful admin tools (essentially a platform at this point). Yeah, there's loads of gameplay I could show off, but like you I would rather not at this point. It looks rough.

Infrastructure, scalability, balance (and the ability to tweak it), plus a visualisation of all aspect of the game systems as an admin tooll. That's not flashy, but is imo essential if you're 'serious' about scaling the game.

Plus, I'd also add the sheer crazy amount of time/effort that goes into balance and bug testings...

Some people are belching out 'full games' in 'let claude do this for 24 hours straight' mode, as if that's actually gonna make a game.

Not a hope in hell.

The AI is a code machinegun. It is not a UI/UX guru. It is not a balance guru. It is not a modularity guru. 

It is a performance guru - but only if you demonstrate performance problems via testing.

Main issue is that AI can't come up an original game idea, story, or ability to balance all of that. Nor does it think 'we need a way to visualise the game logic web as an admin UI'.   
  
So the human must invest heavily in these aspects in order to create a unique and balanced game.

In other words, game dev is still a multi-year process. No one whatsoever will create a 'great game' in 1 day or 1 month of prompting. Not a hope - not a chance of it.

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
> Infrastructure, scalability, balance (and the ability to tweak it), plus a visualisation of all aspects of the game systems as an admin tool. That's not flashy, but is imo essential if you're 'serious' about scaling the game.

The hard and invisible part! I've been creating databases and creating tools for myself to continue to develop the game more efficiently. But yeah... that's not something you can wow the players with. Not something you can post on Twitter and proudly display.

> Main issue is that AI can't come up an original game idea, story, or ability to balance all of that. Nor does it think 'we need a way to visualise the game logic web as an admin UI'.

Tale as old as time; to create a game, you still need to design it. AI is there to help, AI isn't there to create a game for you in one prompt.

comments.author: Officialpolygrafix
comments.body:
I'd love to hear your process. I've been doing the same, and not one shotting- but making a complete business simulation game with AI assistance. I'm a 24 year game dev vet- an artist and designer. I input my GDD for the game and worked out a production plan with Claude, and it's working great. I've learned so much of how to orchestrate this process with AI and refined it well. i'm 46 days in, and my game is about 80% complete. Playable, economics sorted, just being refined. Art and animations being done by me.     
I can see how it would take some time though.  having a well thought out plan before beginning helps a lot. It's the ole waterfall approach, but agile comes into play as you move through and playtest and add things.

replies.author: Kashmakers
replies.body:
80% complete sounds pretty close and hopeful!

My process is... well I never start out with a plan. Never have. I go straight into art, and my first goal is; let's make a character move on screen. Once that is done, I go for the next tiny goal; transfer a character from one map to another. And then another goal, and another, and so on.

But that's just me, I don't work with plans beforehand. Got a pretty good idea of what I want though. Sometimes I just copy over systems from my old game, but improve it. But I can definitely see how it will help for some people for sure.

I do brainstorm a lot with the AI to get my thoughts and goals on track. Then I put a pin in it, so I can create that system later, and focus on more core systems first.

But I suppose, the simple reason why mine is taking so long, is just the scale of it all, it's not a simple game.

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body:
Without a plan or game design doc, it might be why it's taking so long.  
I understand people do things different ways, but it's likely that the reason it's taking so long.  Think of architect that just grabbed some boards and decided to build a home. Maybe after they nail the board together they realize they need a foundation, so they tear the boards down, add a foundation, put the boards back up, then realize they didn't account for plumbing, so now they have to tear down the foundation and boards, then set up some plumbing in the ground then pour the cement.. ect.   It's good to be spontaneous in many instances, but if time, money and patience arent on your side, then putting a little thought into it first with a plan might help prevent backpeddling later. comments.author: Nice_Try4389
comments.body:
You could probably actually speed that up significantly if you take up agile and devops processes and implement the  first into your workflow.  Go in with a clear goal, a clear intention, a set of requirements which say what must and must not be, and set up CI/CD pipelines along with a proper development template for the AI to follow and it will, get you further faster.  And by template I don’t mean pointing it to game design resources, I mean setting up basic rules for it documenting every single thing it does, having it automate the setup of architectural docs, code maps, traceability matrices, and implementing TDD philosophy by having it do red-green test sets for everything it does, along side UI interactions rules can grossly speed things up.  Things like red-green tests means you are only writing the code you need and nothing more.  Similarly by having clearly defined UI interaction standards that means while you may need to change the UI design for better layout or ease of readability the functionality will remain the game.  

For example I ascribe to the philosophy that the players should always be able to immediately see why an action they want to take is not valid through one of several means.  If the action is one they should not be able to take period because none of the requirements are met (wrong phase, not even basic requirement met, etc) then it should not even be presented as an option to the player, if basic requirements are met but something else is outstanding it should be say present in the form of a greyed out or disabled selection which clearly identifies the cause when hovered over, if there is some other action which has caused it to be disabled it should likewise clearly state that action.  By setting up these rules before hand, and others, before development even begins that means it is ALWAYS coding with that intent which again means you aren’t having to tweak the rule, you are simply tweaking the expression of it which I argue is less work then having to find some way to shoehorn in those design philosophies later.   And really that can be applied to anything.   But yeah spend a couple of days setting up a development template that captures the game design philosophies you ascribe to and it can drastically speed everything up on the system’s side.  Leaving art, sound, and sfx as the trouble areas.  Then you can refine and use said design template in future games.  Also I think too many people try to do too big of projects, start small, get a lot of smaller things out while you figure out your actual design philosophy and beliefs for what actually makes a good game and iterate up to what you really want to have taking what went before as your inputs and guidance.  Again you’ll get more done and go further faster, while learning what types of workflows work for you.
